title: Acyclic Conjunctive Queries: Use the Tree Structure
lead: A query can be large yet easier to evaluate because the relationships between its variables have a useful structure.
goals: Build a hypergraph from the query atoms
Check the running-intersection property and apply GYO reduction
Use bottom-up semijoins to answer a Boolean conjunctive query

sections.title: From atoms to hyperedges
sections.html:
The previous lesson showed why arbitrary CQ patterns can be hard. Now ask what makes some patterns easier. Consider Q() :- R(a,b), S(b,c), T(c,d), where a,b,c,d are variables. R shares b with S; S shares c with T. After finding a compatible S tuple, the two end branches have no other shared variable to disagree about. That structure is the opportunity we will exploit.

Represent each variable by a vertex and each atom's complete variable set by a hyperedge: {a,b}, {b,c}, {c,d}. A hyperedge can contain more than two vertices. Keeping that whole set matters: one atom U(a,b,c) checks three values together.

A different diagram connects the atom occurrences themselves: R—S—T. This is a join tree when every variable appears in a connected group of nodes. For b, the nodes R,S are adjacent. For c, S,T are adjacent. For a,d there is just one node each. Equivalently, if a variable occurs at both ends of a tree path, it must occur at every intermediate node. This is the running-intersection property.

Do not mix three diagrams. In a primal graph, vertices are variables and each atom connects every pair of its variables. In a query hypergraph, vertices are variables but hyperedges retain whole atoms. In a join tree, nodes are atoms. Both U(a,b,c) and R(a,b),S(b,c),T(c,a) have a triangular primal graph. Yet the first has a one-node join tree, while the second has no join tree.

The lecture calls a hypergraph acyclic when it has a join tree. Bounded treewidth of primal graphs and bounded hypertree width of hypergraphs describe broader tractable structural classes; acyclicity is the width-one case of the latter. These are restrictions on query structure, not a claim that every CQ has become easy.

Try it: in R(a,b)—T(c,d)—S(b,c), does b pass the path test?

No. b is at R and S but missing from the middle T. The atoms form an ordinary tree, yet it is not a valid join tree. Reorder it to R—S—T to restore the required connectedness.

sections.title: Worked example: a chain and a triangle
sections.html:
Let us test a chain and then change just one atom. For R(a,b)—S(b,c)—T(c,d), the join tree works: b stays on R—S, c on S—T, and a,d occur once. Every variable's occurrences remain connected.

Replace T(c,d) with T(c,a). The hyperedges are {a,b}, {b,c}, {c,a}. A tree on three atom nodes must put one node in the middle. There are only three choices:

Middle nodePath endpointsVariable missing in middle
R(a,b)S and Tc
S(b,c)R and Ta
T(c,a)R and Sb

Every possible tree fails, so this triangle is cyclic. Merely drawing two lines between three atoms cannot fix it.

Now add U(a,b,c) as a fourth atom. Use U as the center and connect R,S,T directly to it. The a nodes are R—U—T; b nodes R—U—S; c nodes S—U—T. All paths retain their variable. The enlarged hypergraph is acyclic, even though its primal graph is still triangular.

Adding U changes the query: U supplies an additional condition and may reduce its result. We are comparing structural properties, not proposing an equivalent rewrite that invents a relation.

Try it: may you add an imaginary U just to use an acyclic evaluation algorithm?

No. A relation U would need defined contents and a proof that the new query preserves answers. Structural tractability alone does not authorize changing the question. For the stated four-atom query, the central-U join tree is valid.

Key takeaway

Check the path of each variable in the proposed join tree. Connecting all the atoms in a tree is not enough. A variable cannot appear at both ends of a path and disappear at an intermediate node.

Sources and teaching scope

Sources: PDF pages 4–13.

sections.title: Apply GYO reduction by hand
sections.html:
Testing all possible trees is inconvenient for larger queries. The GYO reduction recognizes acyclicity by repeatedly peeling away parts that cannot sustain a cyclic dependency. Two operations are allowed: remove a variable appearing in only one remaining hyperedge; remove a hyperedge contained in another. Delete empty edges when they arise.

Here is the complete chain trace. At each step, “only one” refers to the current structure, not the original one.

0: {a,b}, {b,c}, {c,d}
1: {b},   {b,c}, {c}
2:        {b,c}
3:        {c}
4:        {}
5:        ∅

Step 1 removes a,d because each occurs in one edge. Step 2 removes {b},{c} because both are contained in {b,c}. Steps 3 and 4 remove b,c, each now in only one edge. Step 5 deletes the empty edge. Recount occurrences after each structural change.

Reduction to nothing establishes acyclicity. The deletion operations concern the hypergraph used for recognition; they are not instructions to delete query predicates from the application.

For {a,b},{b,c},{c,a}, every variable appears twice and no edge is contained in another. Neither rule applies, so a nonempty remainder persists: the triangle is cyclic. Different valid rule orders can be used; the criterion is complete reduction.

Recognition and evaluation measure different work. With |Q| denoting query size, the lecture presents linear-time acyclicity recognition O(|Q|). Its evaluation bound O(|D|·|Q|) concerns the decision/membership setting and the acyclic algorithm, not printing every possible answer. A bound for one task cannot be silently used for another.

Try it: add {a,b,c} to the triangle and run GYO.

Each two-variable edge is contained in {a,b,c}, so delete those three edges. Each remaining variable occurs only in the single large edge; delete a,b,c and then its empty edge. The reduction succeeds, matching the central-U join tree from the preceding section.

sections.title: Yannakakis: remove tuples that cannot contribute to a result
sections.html:
We can now use the tree to remove candidates that cannot form a complete answer. Use this original database:

R(A,B)={(u,1),(v,2)}
S(B,C)={(1,k),(2,m)}
T(C)={k}

The Boolean query asks whether one assignment satisfies R(A,B),S(B,C),T(C). Choose R as root of R—S—T. Start at the leaf T. S's tuple (1,k) has support in T, but (2,m) does not. Keep only (1,k). Then R's tuple (u,1) has support in the reduced S, while (v,2) does not. The reduced root contains (u,1), so YES: A=u,B=1,C=k is a witness.

The filtering operation semijoin S ⋉ T keeps S tuples having a matching T tuple, but returns only S columns. Unlike a full join it does not append T's columns or duplicate an S tuple for each matching T tuple. We use it to check support, not enumerate witnesses.

A parent needs support from every child

Consider a branch: R(A,B)={(a,1),(b,1),(c,2)}, S(B,C)={(1,k),(2,m)}, T(A)={b,c}, U(C)={k}. Root R has children S,T; S has child U.

S ⋉ U       = {(1,k)}
R ⋉ S       = {(a,1),(b,1)}
(R ⋉ S) ⋉ T = {(b,1)}

The first branch demands B=1. The second demands A be b or c. Only (b,1) satisfies both; witness A=b,B=1,C=k extends through the complete tree. Ignoring T would incorrectly retain (a,1).

Try it: replace T(A) with {c}.

The S branch still leaves {(a,1),(b,1)} at R. Filtering by T={c} removes both, so the root is empty and the answer is NO. R's original (c,2) had support from T but lost support from S. Each child alone had some match; no root tuple has support from both.

Sources and teaching scope

sections.title: Why the tree structure matters
sections.html:
Why may we combine the surviving branches? In a join tree, any variable shared between branches must also pass through their connecting node. Once a parent tuple fixes those shared values, witnesses from separate reduced subtrees cannot introduce a hidden disagreement. Inductively, a surviving root tuple can extend into a full match. This is why the bottom-up semijoin pass answers the Boolean question.

A cycle loses that guarantee. Let R(A,B)={(0,0),(1,1)}, S(B,C)={(0,0),(1,1)}, T(C,A)={(0,1),(1,0)}. Every tuple has a neighbor in each adjacent relation when checked separately. But R requires A=B, S requires B=C, and T requires C≠A. No global assignment exists. Local support does not imply global consistency here.

To test membership of a particular head tuple, first constrain each output variable to its proposed value. Preserve constants and equalities from repeated variables. Each atom occurrence gets its candidate relation after those checks; two occurrences of one base relation are separate roles in the pattern. Then run the Boolean tree procedure.

For the earlier chain, replacing T={k} by T={q} makes S empty and then R empty, so NO. For the branching example, a bottom-up pass only guarantees that surviving root tuples extend through their subtrees. It need not remove every useless tuple at every other node. A top-down pass can finish that full reduction before joining/enumerating answers; that is an additional goal.

The O(|D|·|Q|) bound here is for the presented decision/membership setting. An output query can produce many tuples, and writing them already takes output-proportional time. Do not promise the same bound for enumerating an arbitrarily large result.

Try it: how many tuples does Q(x,y) :- R(x),S(y) output if each relation has n values?

n² pairs. The two independent atoms form an acyclic query, but printing all pairs needs at least n² output work. Boolean existence asks only whether both inputs are nonempty, a much smaller task.

Key takeaway

Returning YES or NO is different from enumerating every answer. A query may produce many output tuples. Printing them alone requires time proportional to the output size.

quiz.question: GYO reduction stops with the triangle {a,b}, {b,c}, {c,a}. What follows?
options: It is acyclic because it has three edges
It is cyclic because reduction cannot eliminate the whole hypergraph
Every possible database must be tested
No query corresponds to this structure
quiz.explanation: No variable has degree at most 1, and no edge is contained in another. The nonempty structure left by GYO reduction establishes that the hypergraph is cyclic.

source.summary: Lecture 25 introduces conjunctive-query graphs and hypergraphs, useful structural classes, join trees, GYO reduction, and Yannakakis’s algorithm for acyclic queries.

limitations: The stated time bound does not include enumerating an arbitrarily large output. This lesson focuses on the decision problem.
